title: Do not covet
hookLine: the only commandment about desire alone

cards: The commandment piles them up one after another, the way an eye moves down a street, over a fence, into somebody else's yard.

And then, as if it knows the list could never be finished, it ends with: anything that is your neighbor's. Read the earlier commandments and they mostly name things a person does: steal, kill, speak falsely.

teach.b: Here it is in the King James Bible: "Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house, thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife, nor his manservant, nor his maidservant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor any thing that is thy neighbour's."
Notice what it doesn't forbid. Wanting a house isn't the problem. Wanting your neighbor's house is: the desire that looks at someone else's life and decides it should have been yours.

The apostle Paul picks out this commandment when he describes what the law showed him about himself. In his letter to the Romans he writes: "I had not known lust, except the law had said, Thou shalt not covet."
Some readers put it this way: his hands might stay clean, but his wanting was another matter, and this commandment brought it into the light. So the Christian answer isn't to stop wanting.
It's contentment, and Paul is honest that it takes practice. To the Philippians he writes: "I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content." Learned.
The letter to the Hebrews gives the ground under it: be content with such things as ye have, for God has said, "I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee."
Coveting says my life is short of something, and the neighbor has it. Contentment says what I have is enough, because I'm not left alone with it. It doesn't mean pretending you lack nothing.
It means you can see your neighbor's good things and leave them where they are.

how: Christians learn this commandment with the rest of the Ten Commandments in catechism and Sunday school, and examine themselves by it in prayer; Paul's words on contentment in Philippians 4 are sometimes read alongside it.

o: not setting your heart on what belongs to someone else
never wanting anything new for yourself at all
a ban on buying more than you truly need

it names what is your neighbor's: the desire that decides their life should have been yours.
Paul says this commandment showed him his own desire
"I had not known lust, except the law had said, Thou shalt not covet."

games.q: you're Paul, writing to the Romans about what the law showed you about your own heart. which commandment do you name?
o: thou shalt not bear false witness.
games.why: Romans 7:7: "I had not known lust, except the law had said, Thou shalt not covet." the commandment about wanting showed him his wanting.

practice: Bring to mind one person who has something you've wanted, a house, a job, a marriage, an easy kind of confidence, and notice whatever stirs in you, without scolding it.
Then, on each slow breath, wish them well in it: their house kept warm, their work going well. If you pray, you can thank God for what they've been given.

wordCard.voice: Do not covet. Don't set your desire on what belongs to your neighbor. The commandment that reaches past the hands to the wanting itself.

orig.note: Hebrew, from Exodus 20:17: do not covet, do not set your desire on it.

carryVoice: Your line: enough is enough. Contentment, Paul says, is something learned, not born. See you tomorrow.
